utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Good morning, sir. Would you please take the card offered you and read allowed the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. Good morning, Mr. Bisic. I'll be asking you questions today as counsel for Mr. Mrksic. Since we both use the same language, could you make a short pause after my question before you start answering so that everything may be accurately recorded. Mr. Bisic, could you please share your personal details with us, your year of birth, place of birth, and so on.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I'm Stevo Bicic. I was born on the 9th of January, 1953 in Perenci, Slavonska municipality, Croatia. After finishing my elementary school education I went on to secondary school after which I spent three and a half years in service. I was then transferred to the Guards Brigade in Belgrade. What used to be Comrade Tito's escorts units. This unit is where I stayed until 1992. I was a low-level official.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In order to be able to follow, what was your training exactly and when did you first start serving with the army?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I finished a traffic junior officers' school in Podgorica, Montenegro, in 1972. In 1972, I also started working professionally as a soldier and an NCO. My first job as a soldier was to command a detachment in Knin. I spent about three and a half to four years there. I then completed a number of specialised courses, and then I joined the Guards Unit, more specifically, Tito's escort unit. We also provided escort for foreign dignitaries visiting Yugoslavia. There was a total of 43 foreign presidents and Prime Ministers visiting for as long as I was there. After Tito died, we continued to provide escort for these high-ranking state and military delegations arriving in the former Yugoslavia. That went on until 1986. In 1986, I joined the anti-terrorist platoon within that same brigade. My term with the unit expired six months before the beginning of the war, but when the war broke out I rejoined that unit and stayed with them until 1992. In 1992, I was transferred from the Guards Brigade. Because I hail from one of the war-torn areas, I returned in 1993 to Vukovar to serve there and stayed there until 1996, which is when the Dayton Accords were signed, upon which I returned to Belgrade whilst for a while serving with a small unit attached to a hospital and was eventually sent into retirement in 2003. So right now I'm a retired NCO of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from the three or four years spent in Knin, the rest of your military career was spent in Belgrade with the Guards Unit. Would that be a fair assumption, sir? Can you tell us about this unit which you belonged? Who did the unit comprise, active duty soldiers as well or just new recruits?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: These were the years when the first anti-terrorist units were being established throughout the former JNA, as far as I know. It was in the 1970s that the first units were set up. We were all in the same compound, and we all knew each other. I was with the special unit in charge of motorcycles and other escort vehicles. Those lads were in the adjacent building. We would often meet. We didn't really talk that much because that just wasn't the done thing in our job, but we knew how they prepared for their tasks and how they worked in general. This unit, as all other units throughout the former Yugoslavia, was being set up, as was the SUP units with which we shared a number of military drills. The programme expanded gradually to include elements from our unit, some of our drivers to be more specific, so that late in 1986, the two of us from the special unit, the vehicle escort unit, joined the organic composition of the anti-terrorist platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned your background in traffic and vehicles. Did you also serve as a driver in this unit or did you serve as a driver in addition to something else? What precisely was your status in this unit?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Which one do you mean, the Anti-Terrorist Unit or the other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the Anti-Terrorist Unit.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I served as an escort driver for the most part, although I had gone through most of the training, as did my other fellow driver. You had to go through all the training in order to become just a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1991 now, which is the period that we focus on. Your anti-terrorist platoon, how many people did it comprise altogether?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I was the second most senior officer in terms of age there, the second oldest. The oldest was a Croat who, unfortunately, died a natural death. I was a warrant officer. That's in terms of biological age. The figure varied, but our strength varied, but by the time we set off for Vukovar, I think there were 32 active-duty officers in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All active duty; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that particular component. There was another component comprising about 45 soldiers, anti-terrorist specialists who had gone through the appropriate training and they made up the other half of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will be focusing mostly on the active-duty component. I'll ask you about the other component too. Were these components multi-ethnic or did one ethnic group predominate?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: It was a typically mixed unit. Not along party lines, I don't mean that. It was mostly about training and background. That's how people were selected based on their qualifications. I don't know what the exact make-up was in terms of figures, but we were all kinds. Two Macedonians. There were a handful of Croats too. Our commander was a Muslim. There were other lads who were members of that unit upright, honest lads, Muslims, as well. There were some people, even until after the war I didn't even know what their ethnicity was, and people eventually told me, and needless to say there were Serbs in the unit too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about your commander a while ago. Do you remember who was the commander of the entire Guards Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. Of course I do. Which specific time do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When all of this was going on in Vukovar, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: The commander was -- he's present here. I recognise him. The commander of the Guards Brigade was Colonel Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember how long he remained commander or, rather, for how long did you remain under his command within the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I remember the first time he arrived. He used to be an officer with the Guards Brigade earlier on. We heard it from our older colleagues. And then he had a tour and stayed with various of our units. I am not quite familiar with the details of that. And then when he arrived again in the Guards Brigade that's an event that I remember well. We all lived within Beli Dvor, which was an official residence of the president, and I remember us playing table tennis when he arrived. I don't remember the year, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. But at any rate, you knew him for a long time as a commander. Would you please briefly describe him as commander. What was he like?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mile Mrksic was an officer with an extremely serious attitude. I met him in the afternoon hours. I didn't know his rank or the post that he came to assume. We just started playing table tennis spontaneously and then continued for a long time without me even knowing his rank. He would come in a tracksuit, so I didn't know what his rank was. I knew that he slept there on the premises, and later on my colleagues told me that he was lieutenant colonel, I think, and then for a while he was Chief of Staff. He was a man of firm principles, of a very responsible, serious attitude. A bit spartan in his upbringing mostly in relationship to himself and also in the way he treated us. The escort unit of the late President Tito had a peculiar Code of Conduct. We had very firm work ethics, but in the military sense we were not super soldiers. We had very well developed work ethics and discipline, though. When Colonel Mrksic arrived, he raised the entire thing at a very -- to a very high level, and we became an elite unit. We received commendation from many international dignitaries who used to come at the time. I perhaps participated less than others. I myself participated in the escort service of 43 visiting heads of states, but I also received some official commendation in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember who served in the post of commander prior to Colonel Mrksic assuming the post?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I think that it was Colonel Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to turn to a different topic, namely your deployment and the deployment of your unit to the Vukovar area. Even though we have information about that, can you tell us about the time when this took place, and where did you go from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I will be speaking about the march of the anti-terrorist platoon, 45 soldiers and 23 officers of this anti-terrorist platoon. We set out within the entire column. We were part of that column. I'm not quite sure about the date, but it could have been the 29th of August or at around that time. When we came to Sid, our group separated itself and we stayed for the night in a motel near a forest. After that, we joined the entire column and continued moving towards Vukovar. En route to Vukovar, what was quite unusual was that we had a baptism by fire, so to speak. It was a minor armed clash near a place called Orolik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just stop my learned friend for one moment? There may be a small problem on translation. It's coming up the second time. Our understanding is that when the word in B/C/S is being translated as a platoon, in actual fact it should be a company, where a company has three platoons and clearly there is an important distinction. I don't know if my learned friend could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Moore. We'll try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you understand the question? Did understand what was not clear to Mr. Moore? When we speak of the Anti-Terrorist Unit, would you please explain whether it's a platoon or a company, or what was it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: The anti-terrorist platoon, when it comes to officers and also to soldiers, I don't know quite the numbers, but our platoon had two -- had 32 officers, and it was called a platoon. As for the soldiers, there were about 40-something soldiers, troops. I'm not sure what it was called, whether it was a platoon. I think that it was also a platoon. So these two components comprised one whole, which was known as a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, this company comprised professional officers, 30-some of them. That was one platoon. And then there was another platoon comprising soldiers, troops, soldiers who were there on their military service, the mandatory military service. And these two platoons together comprised anti-terrorist company; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, let us go back to this place you mentioned, Orolik. You said that you had your first armed clash there, baptism by fire. What kind of an attack was it? Was it an artillery attack or what?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, the place is called Orolik and it is between Tovarnik and Vukovar, on the road between Tovarnik and Vukovar. We were exposed to a mortar attack apparently launched by a small group of Croatian paramilitaries at the time, and they also started sniping. I didn't even notice this, but a colleague sitting next to me or, rather, there was a sniper bullet that just zoomed in front of me. It was a dumdum bullet. I was driving and this bullet zoomed in front of me. And then there was also an intense mortar fire. We halted. A part of our unit organised itself, and they put up resistance, and then we continued on to Negoslavci, which is a place seven to eight kilometres before Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bisic. I will now turn to a different topic, to something that the Defence is interested in, the Defence of Mr. Mrksic, namely the day of the fall of Vukovar. Do you remember which day is considered as the day that Vukovar fell, and do you remember that day? And then I will continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: As was my habit, I used to read various documents available to me, mostly press releases. Some people mentioned the 19th, some people mentioned the 18th. As was popularly called, we were at the top, at the -- at the forefront of the events at the time, and as far as I'm aware, the definite fall of Vukovar was on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The 18th. All right. Can you tell us what you remember about that day? On the 18th in the morning, what did you do and what was taking place?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: All right. The 32 officers within our unit were constantly, from the 2nd of October when we enter the city, in attack operations, and even though those people were top of the line professional soldiers with excellent training, they naturally were also prone to human weaknesses, to various psychological traumas, and this ultimately led to our unit being weakened. We were quite weakened at the end. And the posts vacated by officers were then filled by soldiers who, as I told you, were prepared to come there on a voluntary basis. One could tell even earlier that Vukovar was going to fall, but that very morning -- I can't describe the situation with hundred per cent accuracy. Most of us didn't expect that it was precisely that day that Vukovar was going to fall. Sometime in the morning hours we had a major action, and there were other actions taking place around us, and this was all rumbling altogether so to speak so at some points we didn't even know what was going on. Then we heard that the surrender was about to take place, and that then we heard that the surrender was actually taking place, that it was in progress. Apparently their elite units, which served at the front line and who on the radio were referred to as Paraga's Red Berets. It was those units that were supposed to surrender. If we go back a bit to the beginning, I have to tell you that they nicknamed me Caruga. And then in the very beginning, since we used radio communication with the Croatian unit, it was a simplex channel, that's what it was called, a Croatian officer used to communicate with me, and it progressed to that point -- to the point where we would normally chat two or three times a day, and we would chat about basic, ordinary things, even going into such details as, "What did you have for lunch?" and so on. It was a respectful communication, and I talked to him the last time on the 15th or the 16th. And then we started telling each other semi-truths. Between the night -- on the night between the 15th and 16th, we talked for the last time, and then on the 17th I tried to radio him and asked him how was the night. You know, "Did you have breakfast?" But he didn't respond. And then on the 18th the same thing. And we heard that the surrender was in progress, and we heard that there was an order to seize all major attacks, because the surrender was in progress. The units were ready to surrender. Another confirmation of their readiness to surrender, the readiness of the command staff, came from Colonel Panic, who had arrived. Two of our members of special forces climbed up the water tower and raised the Yugoslav flag there. It was quite difficult for us to locate that flag, because that was in the territory held by Croatians. I know that it took us a long time to locate the flag. Finally they did, and then these young men took down the Croatian chequerboard flag and raised the Yugoslav flag. I know that Colonel Panic radioed that they were not allowed to climb the water tower because it was quite risky. We had heard that there was still active snipers in the area, so that's why he told him that. And then all of a sudden at one point we could see the Yugoslav flag flying above the water tower. At that time, I found myself near the outskirts of Vukovar, near the Danube Hotel. I remember that on the bridge there was a young man, a soldier of ours who had wounded himself accidentally. His rifle was aimed downwards, and he accidentally fired in his own foot. And then in the afternoon hours at the hospital the surrender was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. To be quite sure, you are now referring to the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember any event in the morning or in the afternoon in the centre of Vukovar where you yourself were?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: When it comes to morning hours, my memory's a bit foggy. I don't know the chronology quite well. But as for the afternoon when that soldier wounded himself, what I remember from that time was that I was radioed to come urgently to the Danube Hotel. When I came there, I found a group of our soldiers and four imprisoned Croatian soldiers in front of them. My colleagues said, "Here, you take them." I was a bit angry, because they had made me interrupt a task that I was doing at the time. (redacted) naturally ordered me and my conscience told me I should go where the situation was the most difficult. So other soldiers and I were transporting people from a basement, mostly the elderly, elderly ladies and so on. It was very difficult to evacuate them and -- from that basement. So this soldier was trying to lighten up the atmosphere, saying that these old ladies had 90 years and 90 kilos. And we -- and we were evacuating them. And then they interrupted me in that task to go fetch these four soldiers. So I was a bit angry, and I was saying, "Why did you call me in? Couldn't you have solved it in another way?" However, I loaded them onto Puch vehicle. One of them, it seemed as though his brain was exposed. He had absolutely no hair, and then this part of the head was all wrinkled up so I couldn't say whether that was some kind of an infection or whether his brains were actually exposed. At any rate, they entered the Puch vehicle. The soldier with those wrinkles on his head was lying down, and then there was another man, elderly, large, quite large, and I remember that he had a crooked nose, he sat in front and then his son sat next to him. And then a guy who was quite strongly built, with longish hair, sat next to me. I didn't make them face down. We searched them, and then we made them hold -- hold a part of the vehicle and keep their heads straight without moving it left or right. Our soldiers found quite a lot of items, among them, parts of uniforms of Praga's soldiers who wore black shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a minute. First of all, I'd like to ask you to slow down for the sake of interpretation, and then I'd like to remind you of what we said in the beginning, to refrain from mentioning any names. I think that you did mention a name. Please continue, but please focus on what you did with the captured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: All right. The chronology. People started celebrating in town. Our units were joined by those who were not in immediate, direct combat, and that near an intersection in town, near a chapel there, I saw our soldiers, our soldiers from the anti-terrorist platoon had unusual helmets, and then this soldier of ours saw the Puch vehicle and he ran to me very enthusiastically to greet me. In the meantime, I inquired of the guy who sat next to me. He told me his name, but I forgot it. I told him my name. I told him what my position was, and I asked him where he was from. He said literally that he was born and lived in Vukovar for a year, and then he went silent. And I asked him, "Then? What happened then?" He said, "Well, I went to Germany, and then I came back to defend my homeland." I extended my hand and congratulated him, and I told him that he was a good Ustasha. I congratulated him in the vehicle there. In the meantime, we came across this soldier I mentioned. He was running towards us, and he got confused by the black uniform. He thought that he was one of our guys and then just changed clothes. This soldier was a Muslim. I don't remember his first name, but he was nicknamed Zvaljo, which is quite a nasty nickname. I asked people not to call him that but he didn't mind himself. He was a very brave, nice guy. I told this Croat, greet this fighter. He came running towards us, arms opened wide, and the two of them greeted each other and pecked each other on the cheek, that sort of thing. So this other soldier probably thought that I'd been trying to set him up, but then I took them both to the command in Negoslavci and surrendered them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So there were four of these captured soldiers. You took them to Negoslavci and surrendered them to the command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I surrendered them there and they weren't mistreated or anything, not that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What did you do later?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: We continued evacuating the people who couldn't walk. I also got some footage from someone. I have no idea who -- who filmed these infirmed people being brought into the vehicle. At dusk the commander called me and told me to come over to the school building. There was another soldier with me in the Puch, and as we reached the school building we realised there was some of our own boys there. They had caught a pig, and they set it up for roasting on what a -- what do you call that? You know. It was in the -- it was in the concourse of the school building, and it had been destroyed. There was a group of about 15 people there or thereabouts. I can't be more specific. The school building is a huge, enormous building, and we toured the building and we found a room in it that was full of helmets, which we were surprised to find. In another room we found rations. In yet another room we found supplies of oil. And then the commander told me, Caruga, "Let's go get the commander. Let's call Mrksic. Let's call him over. We'll get him a diary. Rather, we'll get him a school register. He went to school here. Let's find the register so we can see what kind of marks he had back then." And he did call him. Do you believe that? But Mrksic never did come. I don't know why he didn't come. He was probably busy elsewhere. And we couldn't find the register. This pig was being roasted for a total of three hours. Just before the end, just before it was nearly done, the commander leapt to his feet. He said, "Quick, let's go. Let's go to Ovcara." We said, "Why Ovcara?" And he said, "Well, the word is spreading, there's something going on there." I was the first to get into the vehicle, and then he came with me, and then all the other lads got into their vehicles. I -- I think there were a total of four vehicles. As fast as we could, we were off to Ovcara. It was dusk already. It was on the 18th of November. The season was autumn, and it was getting dark already. We reached Ovcara. We literally dashed out of our vehicles and there was some military policemen waiting for us there. All of us, not for ethnic reasons or anything, weren't really shaving regularly in those days. Not because we were making a point but because we hardly had time for a place to wash, so we all had beards. All of us, Croats, Serbs, and the few Muslims alike. No one shaved regularly in those days. It wasn't an ideological thing. It wasn't something to strut. We just didn't shave. I have mentioned this before. So it's nothing ideological. And we didn't have our ranks displayed. This police commander tried to take it out on me because my beard was white. I was 38 at the time. I had quite a beard. He thought I was the most senior officer there in terms of rank. He probably thought that. He came up to me and I said, "Don't -- don't touch these people." I just walked past him, and I said, "Get off my chest, Captain." He was a captain by rank, obviously. He just kept repeating the same thing. He followed me and he said, "There's been an order from Belgrade that these people must not [realtime transcript read in error "the"] be touched, so don't touch them." I turned to face him. I told him to get lost, and I said, "I'll throw you among them." And then the captain backed off. And all of us, the whole unit, walked into the hangar. It's quite a long room. On the right-hand side of the hangar the door was ajar. It's a sliding door, I think. And it wasn't quite open. There was a Pinzgauer just outside with its headlights -- with its headlights on, and these headlights were pointed at a group of captured Croats. We exchanged a few comments in our own private language, and we said, "Are these guys or ours?" That's what we meant. Our Ustashas, why our Ustashas, because they were along our front line and they kept withdrawing, withdrawing, withdrawing, and they just handed themselves over to the regular units. But there was a very thin -- there was a length of very thin rope running between where they were and the far end of the hangar. The room was approximately this big, like this part of the room over here. We went in with no orders being issued. There was no one issuing orders. We just dropped our rifles on the ground. And once inside they started regrouping and running in a certain direction. We stood right there in the middle of this hall, the hangar. They separated so a funnel-like space was created. We came in from the left. There was stacks of hay there, a lot of hay, and further down a couple of armed soldiers. We reach the middle of the room, and they had split up in two groups. A tall, young man came forward, introduced himself as Big Dzo. They were all wearing civilian clothes and all of them were clean shaven, nearly all of them. I don't recall seeing one who had a beard, and most of them had jeans on. He said his name was Big Dzo. He walked up to one of our own officers, Aziz Memic, the Muslim, and said in a strict voice, "Please make sure you stick to the Geneva Conventions now." He was a tall man, and Memic is very short. So this man bent down in order to speak to him directly, to face him. Memic just kept silent for a while, and then he told him to get lost. And then this man returned to his group and blended with the mass of people there. In the meantime, one of our own men had brought over a power generator to be used for the lighting. He connected a capable through the window, and the far part of the capable was finishing in the end of the room where the Croats were. This man setting up the circuit was not supposed to pass underneath the cable. He was trying to tie it up. And I told him, "Just go over there and do the usual thing." And once he did I realised there was some neon lights in the hall from before, so the whole room was lit up. You could see everything that was going on there. Most of our lads had left by this time. I was one of the few people left. I was just looking around, not really believing that I would recognise anybody. You could tell just by looking at those men that they were fully trained. There was one among them who struck me as being there by mistake. It seemed obvious to me at the time, so I told him to come outside. But a different man would come forward every time, not the one that I wanted. And I said, "You, fat one, come out." So I pulled the rope up for him, and he came with me. I told him who I was. I shook his hand, and he told me his name was Jura. I said, "Jure, where did you come from?" He was paralysed by fear, rooted to the spot. He said, "Zagreb." I patted him on the shoulder and said, "Why are you that scared? You people from Zagreb are good fighters. Everybody knows that." I wasn't being menacing or anything. It was in a friendly way that I patted him. And then he said, "I wasn't involved in the fighting. That's what Croats say. I'd driven my truck over here," and then he was captured there, handed a rifle and said to him, "Jure, now you will have to fight," but he said, "I didn't." I asked him not to lie. I asked him if there were any problems that he had. He said, "None." I asked him again, "Any problems?" He said, "Maybe I should go and urinate." I apologise to the Court. Without meaning to offend him, I asked if he wanted to do it right there or outside. That was cornfield just outside. And he was just petrified. He was probably afraid that I would shoot him. And I said, "Feel free to say where you want to do it. You want to do it right here or in the cornfield over there?" He was just dumb-struck. He didn't say anything. I said, "Well, do it right here." So he urinated on those stacks of hay over there. At one point in time, it dawned on me that he might be trouble just because he was so scared. And I myself was beginning to get scared that he might be trouble for me, because I was certain at the time that the soldiers hadn't searched them probably and frisked them properly. For quite a while I couldn't see him so I didn't know what he was doing, and then I realised that he was wearing black tights underneath the jeans, the kind worn by all members of Paraga's unit. So I understood that he was a nationalist. I felt a rage swell up inside me. I said, "Stop," and I saluted him in a soldierly way, and then we came out of the hangar and we talked. And that's the end of the story. And I don't know. We ended up with that pig over there. Where I slept, believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean to interrupt the witness. I believe there was a mistranslation on page 18, lines 4 and 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the word not was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I was waiting for a time to mention it. On line 5, he said that an order had come from Belgrade that these people must not be touched. The word "not" was not in the transcript. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It's really impossible for me to follow the transcript even was I examine the witness, so I would like to ask you, Witness, to answer very slowly lest we should have some more interpretation errors. I think that you gave us a very detailed account of these events, and in the end you speeded things up a bit because you mentioned the pig, so you were probably talking about the return to Vukovar, so I would like to go back with you. When you left the hanger, all of you who had gone in had gone out; is that correct? Please wait. Or did somebody leave earlier? So you went in as a group and you left as a group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As a group. As a unit that went in, so the entire group went in and went out and came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned the captain that you had a conversation with. Could you describe the uniform he was wearing, whether there was anything peculiar that you might remember?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, they had those striking white belts, the police markings. They were obviously new. There was a Pinzgauer nearby, and in the shadow of its headlights, it was not a very bright light and the darkness was not really very dark. So this man was wearing a uniform. We had different uniforms that we changed. This one was a flannel uniform. That was not the old type of fabric that had been used before. So he was not wearing the camouflage uniform as worn by the special units. He was not so tall, a smallish guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that there were some armed soldiers guarding this group, and my question to you is whether you noticed any other people there, Territorial Defence member -- members or any other groups of people armed or unarmed.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: In the hangar and around the hangar we did not see anyone. En route not to Ovcara, but we would encounter perhaps just a couple of vehicles. I can not now say with any certainty that we did not encounter any vehicle or anyone, but we did not see any people up there apart from the military police that guarded the facility in a proper formation deployed as they should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question to you was whether you saw any other people in front of the hangar or perhaps in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you from the conversations of the people or what people were saying, those in the hangar or the people who were guarding them, did you perhaps hear where those prisoners had come from.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: The figure that was bandied about was 86. I don't recall who actually gave that figure, but this is something that I remember that stuck in my memory, 86, and that these were Praga's special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was there any mention as to what part of Vukovar they had come from, where they had been captured?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: From what I was able to learn from the commander, they had been on the axis of our attack. That's where they were deployed. They withdrew across Mitnica, and they surrendered to the young soldiers. Hence what -- the rumour that spread. These are our people, our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that's what you heard on that occasion, and I believe that you said that you had heard that from the commander. Was it your commander or who, who it was?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the man that I was in communication. I don't know whether he was a squad leader, but I think that I heard it from him, because I talked to him most, and we spent the most time together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you came in in four Pinzgauer vehicles, that you came in in an organised way, and you said that you had returned in the same organised manner. On your way back, in other words, when you departed from Ovcara, did you see anything peculiar or perhaps hear anything of interest?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, nothing special. When we got to the high school, the -- the commander and myself, we saw an unexploded howitzer shell, and we actually -- our vehicle came across that howitzer shell. This really shook us up. But I don't recall anything that would be out of the ordinary. Well, when I say "ordinary," in those days very few things were ordinary. The whole town had fallen, had collapsed. There were dead and wounded all around. But this was, in fact, ordinary at the time. This was our everyday life at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you remember that detail when you got back to Vukovar already, but my question referred to an earlier period of time when you departed from Ovcara. So did you hear at that time when you were still in the Ovcara area, did you hear any gunfire?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, nothing out of the ordinary. There was the rumble of gunfire in the distance but nothing that would strike us as being very close. Nothing remarkable really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you correctly, you came -- you arrived back to the same place where you had left from, the place where the pig was being roasted. Did you stay there? Did you have dinner there? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: We stayed there until the early hours of the morning. We stayed there. We ate the meat. We swapped tales. We sat there. I insisted that the tunnels, the maze of tunnels underneath should be checked. Most people said there was nothing dangerous there. And in that evening, that night, nothing special really happen. We were fully prepared to launch any engagements if necessary, but there was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke at the beginning about the events in Vukovar and wounding, I think, you mentioned the snipers. Did the opposite side, the Croatian side, had some snipers and was that a big problem?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes. Their snipers, in fact, caused the most trouble for us, especially in the end-game. The Zelena Ulice, the Green Street, the reporters from SkyNews actually filmed that. I think he's from Holland. His name is Lynden. Mr. Srdjan Kusavac, he was from Radio Free Europe. The headquarters actually sent him to us. I think they spent either two days and three nights or three nights -- or three days and two nights with us. And they were allowed to film almost anything. In fact, they were able to film everything. They were very brave. They went with us to the very front line, and their cameraman, I personally asked him -- I took off my bullet-proof vest. He went to the Ruthenian church, and I asked him not to go there. I pleaded with him, because I said that there was very intense gunfire there. I took off my bullet-proof vest, and Mr. Van Lynden knew me well because he had spent quite a lot of time with us, and the cameraman threw down the bullet-proof vest. He didn't want to take it and then he went to do a thing in church and he was shot with a sniper bullet. I think he had to have his kidney removed because of the wounding. And one of our soldiers drove him to the hospital in Negoslavci, and Mr. Lynden, who was the head of the team and myself, and we got kind of friendly. Not friendly. I was simply amazed by his bravery, because he, a tall man, went about without a bullet-proof vest. And he used to cross the Green Street at a run, although it was constantly exposed to the sniper fire. And then I, although I was shorter than he was, I always said, "Lynden, please allow me to give you some protection." And then the two of us would cross the street ten times or so every day, and he refused to wear a bullet-proof vest at all. We had quite a few casualties on that street, and some of those events were quite horrific.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. This was my question about snipers. Obviously on the 18th there were no snipers any more on the 18th, but were you afraid of all kinds of mines? Did you have problems with them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were very many mines there. There were those pockets of mines that caused us a great deal of problems. You had large areas where there were no mines and then there would be a house or two that were mined heavily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You described in detail your departure and your stay at Ovcara. After that day, you were talking about the 18th, so after that day until the end of you stay in Vukovar, did you go back to Ovcara at any time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. No. I and the rest of the unit, what remained of the unit, we did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you did not go there personally, but are you -- do you know whether your commander or your unit went there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot say that with any certainty, but I'm inclined to believe that they did not go. That seems more likely than that they did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember the date until which you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that on that day we asked -- or maybe that was the next day. We asked for the situation to be clarified to us. The town had fallen. We were physically, totally exhausted. And I often drove the commander to consult with the people at the headquarters and to receive orders, and then he told me that the commander was probably going to receive the next orders, but he cannot make it more specific as to -- until what time we have to stay here. He is going to Belgrade to get his orders, and then when he comes back we'll know the details. So we went back on the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please tell me, as far as you know, did Colonel Mrksic ever come to Vukovar from Negoslavci until the end of your stay there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I saw Colonel Mrksic there very rarely. I used to come to Negoslavci because we had a lot of wounded there. But as far as I know, he never ever entered the Vukovar. His chief of staff came a few times, the staff officers came a few times, but I did not see Colonel Mrksic. I was in the area from the barracks, that extended from the barracks. I was there with the Croatian officer, junior lieutenant, and we often wondered how it came that we had more casualties in the rear than on the front lines, and there was this Croat, a junior officer, and we had to provide him with assistance. We moved a lot in this area between Negoslavci and Vukovar, and we knew almost every day how many people got in and how many left, and I did not see Colonel Mrksic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. At that time he was a Colonel. But you said that other officers, Chief of Staff, did you mean the Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade, Panic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Or did you mean anyone else?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Just before the very end he came to the barracks. In fact, he gave me his armoured fighting vehicle. We didn't have any vehicle to transport the weapons and the ammunition, so he gave me his vehicle and his driver. Our vehicles and our crew, our crews, we had two vehicles. The soldiers had been wounded. One of them was a Croat from Bosnia. He had been wounded by a sniper in the eye area, and he didn't want to go to the hospital. A couple of us insisted, and we forced him to go to hospital, and we didn't have a vehicle, and Panic gave us a vehicle and a driver. We had some problems there. They got stuck. But that was just before the very end. And he came to visit us on foot. He came to visit those troops that were not in direct engagement, that were resting after fighting -- after the fight. And I saw Mr. Sljivancanin a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a Croat soldier originally from Bosnia that had been wounded. Was it your soldier or was it the soldier from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: This soldier was a member of the crew of an armoured fighting vehicle, and he was a gunner. And when they were transporting food to the soldiers at the front line, I was on that vehicle, and he was hit by a dumdum bullet from a sniper. I saw because he was above me, I saw that there was blood streaming down his face from beneath his eyes, and I pulled him into the vehicle. We threw all the food out, and I ordered the driver of the vehicle to turn back and drive back immediately. The barracks was quite close, and we put the soldier into the Puch vehicle, and the soldier did not want to go to hospital, but we forced him to go there. In the end, I learned that his injuries were quite severe and that they really had to put in a lot of effort to save his eyesight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you explained -- when you told us what you remembered about the events of the 18th, you said that you had driven the four captured soldiers to Negoslavci. My question is whether you actually drove to Negoslavci on previous occasions and, if yes, when?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: This love, this is something that brought me into this unit, because with most of these lads, and especially with the commander, I was on very, very good terms. We were not really friends, but we had those really good -- we had this really good relationship, and my emotions made me join them and go back to Vukovar with them, and they were also trying to talk me into that. And that's how I went there. I was not a brave fighter, but it would happen from time to time -- it -- actually, it happened that we were complementary, that we fit with each other well, even the commander. And anyone who tells you that there is no fear is a liar unless they are using tranquilisers. We all had our fears. We were plagued by those thoughts, our personal drama. And then somebody would really fall under the spell of those emotions. I continued socialising with the commander. He believed in me. He would have never deserted him nor he me. And this is how we went for briefing and for orders to Negoslavci. The town was rather small and there was some really dangerous locations, so any move represented a significant risk. We had full trust in each other, and this is why he normally took me to go with him to get orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you drove him from Vukovar to Negoslavci to give reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on what you know, was your commander in attendance? Did he attend the meetings of all officers there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the command of the Guards Brigade, operations group south. Commander was Colonel Mrksic, and then there was the senior -- there were the senior officers there. I didn't attend the meetings. Maybe I entered premises once or twice. Normally, I would be outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you took your commander there, you drove him, do you know whether he went there every day or he would skip some days?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, no, we didn't go every day. I don't remember the exact schedule, but I think he went there when invited, when asked to attend, or if he had something unresolved, he would go to see Colonel Mrksic or any other senior officers. He had an unrestricted access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So your answer is he didn't go every day, but you don't know what the exact intervals were, and you think that he went there when invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that it's time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, are you at the end or near the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very close to the end, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We will adjourn now. There's been a redaction, so we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bisic, in the course of your answers, at one point you also mentioned the Geneva Convention. During your training or during these events, were you given instruction on the application of Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: It is quite natural for every professional soldier to receive not only information but also to be duty-bound to implement provisions of the Geneva Conventions in their service. Naturally, that applied to us as well, this duty. We received instruction on the provisions of the Geneva Conventions back when we had our training and later on when we just started working. During the Vukovar events, we believed that a notebook, rather small one, was circulated even too many times. I think that three times altogether it reached us. Maybe once before we left for Vukovar and then two times while we were in Vukovar. And I think that we even had to sign a receipt indicating that we had received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You made a gesture while describing this notebook. Was it a kind of a brochure on the provisions of the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a type of a pamphlet or a brochure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the brochure that you received not once but, as you indicated, maybe as many as three times during your stay there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bisic, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Bisic, I have one or two questions for you. You've told us that you remember the number 86, the number of the people at Ovcara; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody, and my memory is a bit foggy on this, somebody mentioned the figure of 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would it be right to say, having been in the hangar, that the number of people that you saw in the hangar would have fitted that number?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, if we try to reconstruct the event, we could probably establish that. That area was a bit wider than this area, and then the depth was as the distance between me to this window, and that area was full. So I would say that the number is approximately right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of the people in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the people in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've used the word "commander" for the gentleman whose name you know you cannot give, and I want to ask you questions about him. He's known as 001, all right? So we'll call him 001, or your commander. Do you understand? So we don't mention his name.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I had a number of commanders at various levels. There was a group commander who had eight people under him, and then there was -- yes, I suppose you're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we understand exactly who we're talking about, I'm going to ask to go into closed session. We'll mention the name, and we'll refer to him as the commander thereafter. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You described your commander at the very outset as an exceptionally able officer. Why did you describe him that way? What were the characteristics that you considered made him exceptionally able?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: First of all, he is a man of very high-level mental and physical abilities, which are way above average. In addition to that, he's a man of high moral principles at the time that he displayed in various circumstances, in various missions. During peacetime, we went frequently together on missions. And this is not just my opinion. This is the opinion that prevailed almost unanimously. In the entire unit. It wasn't a respect borne out of fear, no. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that he is an honest man?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That he is an intelligent man?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: All of us are intelligent more or less. I don't know his IQ, but definitely a smart guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you for the compliment for us all. And what about careful? Would you suggest -- would you agree that he is a careful man? He was a careful officer?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you and he got on well together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Exceptionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's also right to say that you accompanied him to Bosnia, I think on two occasions, to collect members of either your or his family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I don't know the source of information, but you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's right to say that that was an extremely dangerous trip. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you both went together. Would it be right to say that in actual fact he was a man who was prepared to risk his life for his fellow soldiers and non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm the one -- I'm one of the people who responded equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, even though it may not seem terribly important to others, I think he was excellent in sport and was well known for his excellence in sport at that time.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to sport, we were top rate, and I think that in the military decathlon his record still stands. He is known in the circles of both older and younger athletes as the top-rate performer. I think that for several years in a row he was the army champion on decathlon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I want to read a definition of what the function is of the counter-terrorist platoon. It's transcript page 10076. I'd like you to listen to this, please, and see if you agree with it. The question was as follows: "What was the function, then, of the counter-terrorist platoon?" Answer: "The counter-terrorist platoon conducted training on a daily basis for anti-terrorist struggle. It also provided security and escort for top-ranking military as well as buildings of strategic importance. This daily training was quite intense. Certain model situations were played out, as it were, such as might occur in the course of anti-terrorist struggle. This included drills such as freeing hostages from stationary or mobile vehicles and other more specific types of training, including target practice, training and using different kinds of weapons, as well as other types of equipment including electronic equipment." Now, that was a definition given. While it's a very long definition, is there anything in it that you would disagree with?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, within that framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the -- if I may use a rather vulgar phrase, the guts of your evidence about the guards is they were quite simply the best of the best. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That was the method of selection applied. Young men who achieved below-average results were not selected. This was a process of natural selection. So only the top ones who were at the top of the pyramid were selected, and that included the unit which provided security. And as for the Anti-Terrorist Unit, the name itself implied top-quality people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I accept that the counter-terrorist company or unit was actually the elite of the guards. Now, do you agree with that? They were the best soldiers selected?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And your commander was one of the very best of them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not one of the best but the best. He was the best, not one of the best. It was all governed by fair rules, and whenever he felt that somebody else was better, he would defer to them. That was the spirit that prevailed at the time, and this was the spirit of spartan attitude, fair play, in addition to the military spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: One of the topics, one of the duties that you would probably have had to deal with was, as I've already mentioned to you, the freeing of hostages. You were trained specifically for that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when one is dealing with a hostage situation, I would suggest to you there are two principal requirements. The first would be what I will call patience or preparation, and the second is decisive action. Would you agree with those? I'm not saying it's absolute, but as two general principles.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with a situation that you had to deal with, I would suggest, where there was a -- there was information that a group of TO volunteers were refusing to fight and were on their way from Vukovar to Negoslavci, and I would suggest that yourself, your commander, and some others went to intercept them. Do you remember that situation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: There were several such situations. I'm not sure which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let me see if I can assist you. It's TO members between Negoslavci and Vukovar. I think they were on their way to Serbia. You were the driver. There were two jeeps. I think a gentleman called Sinikovic was involved, and they wouldn't let their weapons go --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That there were two jeeps. There was your commander, two jeeps. You stopped these volunteers, and it was a situation where you were firm but fair, and your commander took the weapons off the TOs and let them go.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, the situation is a little more complex. The commander was dealing with general questions of command, and we were all dealing with things at ground level, as it were. There were several Muslim soldiers among these. One of them was made Fazlic and another Ibrahimovic. Ibrahimovic was a liberal fellow, and Fazlic was a bit of a poet. It really amazed me that he had the courage to function under those difficult circumstances, and I focused on that particular soldier especially. His compulsory military term had expired already and he should have been home by now. The commander was adamant that the soldier be released but he refused. He said, "I don't want to go," and that was that. A problem arose and I said (redacted), you deal with this because you’re to blame for this situation. I spoke to a couple of my fellow soldiers, and I found out that they had not spoken to their families about this. I put them in a vehicle and drove them to the headquarters to get on the phone to their parents, Ibrahimovic was the first to speak. It was an emotional conversation and that was that. When Fazlic called it was pure drama. His mother was weeping. It was all sadness, sorrow and grief. And he asked me can I tell my mum where I am, and I said sure, go ahead, and he told her where he was. It wasn't before now that she was really grief-stricken. And then she told him could she send him a parcel and he told her what to include in the parcel and that was that. And his mother was encouraged by this, and then we drove back to Vukovar with these lads and it was then that we came across -- or, rather, on the way back the commander joined us and this fellow that you mentioned, and then we came across this group of fugitives and I was adamant that the soldiers should introduce themselves, those soldiers, those, those, and state their ethnicity. And then the solder said what his ethnicity was. I asked the other one. I looked at their papers to go with them. Here these people are off to Belgrade. You go with them or up there at the front, and without any second thoughts the soldiers just proceeded and walked in front. But some of them wanted to get into our vehicle, which we refused to allow them to do, and then the commander seized their weapons and sent them packing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have the good fortune from coming from the Balkans. I have the good fortune of coming from Ireland. We both talk a lot. Can we just try and keep -- you keep your answers short and I'll keep my questions short. Shall we try? Would it right to say --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: That's my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Would it be right to say, however, that the -- that your unit was used when there were urgent situations?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if a situation suddenly I'll use the word brewed up or bubbled up, your unit had the good fortune of trying to sort it out. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so when your commander, when you were relaxing in Vukovar, turning the pig on a spit, it was your commander then who said, "We have got to go to Ovcara." Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to just deal with that if I may, because you said that he leapt to his feet. Does that mean that you were trying to suggest it was urgent?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. No. There was no questions off. When he said we're off, that's the way it was. Urgent meant clapping his palm. If he did that twice, that meant very urgent. He would clap his palm twice, and that spelt urgency. The remaining situations you might define as half urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the double clapping of the hand I'll try that with my children and see if it works. All right? But let's just look then at that situation. You said then in actual fact that word is spreading that something is going on there at Ovcara. That's what you told us.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, excuse me. He didn't slap us with his palm twice. He said, "I'll see if that works with my children," because that's the interpretation I received. I was talking about the level of urgency. Sometimes when we had to be off, no questions asked, he would sometimes do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Clearly my fault. My misunderstanding. But when he referred to Ovcara, he also said that there was something going on there.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: He said there was something going on there. Something along these lines, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Along what lines? What was happening at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: That something was going on. It wasn't very defined. Whether someone had been attacked or what, he didn't say anything special.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did it suggest that there was something wrong going on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I can't say now what the intentions were behind what he said. He said it curtly, in a soldierly manner. There was indications that there was something going on there. Whether that was part of a withdraw by a military group or whatever because there were random groups committing serious crimes, those who refused to surrender and they were creating a lot of trouble for our soldiers. There was all sorts of things going on. But specifically, we didn't have anything very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then what do you mean by the phrase that "word is spreading"? "Word is spreading that something is going on."

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: (redacted) stood up. It was nothing special. He said, "Off we go." "Where?" "To Ovcara." He said, "There's some indication that something is going on over there." No questions asked. We just leapt to our feet, we got into our vehicles, and we were off to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I want to stick on the point. "Word is spreading." You said it in your evidence, and I'm asking you, the phrase "word is spreading," does that mean that it was spreading around that something was happening?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: By this time it was really nothing alarming. It was simply the fact that we were given an order to go to Ovcara to see what was going on. That's all it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then, let's move on in time. Here you have gone to Ovcara and nothing's going on from what you say. Didn't you say to your commander, "Why on earth have we been brought over to Ovcara and there's nothing going on here at all? My dear commander, we have wasted our time. What was this rumour all about?"

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: There was quite certainly something going on over there. Once the combat was over, what happened was that we saw a rather large group in one place of the enemy soldiers who had surrendered, or whatever they were. So even that can be defined as something going on. As I say, we spent some time there, and I've given you the chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I'm asking you, there you went across. There's absolutely nothing happening, from what you say, and I'm asking you did you ask your very good friend, "What was all the fuss about? Why have we come across? There's absolutely nothing unusual here."

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Truth to tell, our amazement and our analysis of the situation boiled down to this: Why didn't they surrender to us? They were near us. This was, after all, an unusual move on their part. They went the long way around only to surrender to young recruits. That was the line of reasoning that prevailed among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well. Let me approach it another way. Did you fight in the Mitnica area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: We didn't cover that area. Maybe towards the end. Some of it, I'm not sure where it lies, I'm not sure about its geographical extent or its street, but I would say, no, certainly not the middle part of Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you knew of Mitnica at that time, didn't you, that it was a strong area for the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you saying that this group of 86 people were from Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: For a clever commander, dynamics is part of both victory and defeat. Was this group from Mitnica? I don't know. The first day of the incursion, I heard the Hawks's voice, Jastreb's voice, he was calling Dedakovic asking him to send the Mungos unit in. So these groups were converging from all sorts of areas into this area. The Mungos unit were the paramilitaries, were the special soldiers belonging to paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But are you saying this group was from Mitnica? Did you ask, for example?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I don't know where that group was from, where they were fighting. They withdrew from our area. Supposedly they crossed Mitnica and they surrendered to those soldiers and that's how they reached Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with your knowledge. You did not ask where that group came from. You're only assuming; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: None of us asked. There were many groups in motion, moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know who the best-known officer in Mitnica was? Did you know his name? Filip Karaula?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Not Karaula, Karaula. Yes, I have heard of him but that's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you were aware of his name on the 18th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I heard about that on the radio. I didn't meet him. I heard his name over the radio equipment that we were using.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you were aware of the name of Filip Karaula on the 18th. Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. Not particularly. Subconsciously, yes, I was aware of that name, but on that day he wasn't a remarkable presence, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So there was no one in that group who came across as the commander, no one in that group of Croatian prisoners who was the commander. There was no commander as such; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: At least in the instances that I saw, none of them declared themselves as such. As I told you, from this group, a man came out and introduced himself as Big Dzo and then he gave that speech, and then there was a man who was one of the fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I asked you a very simple question. When you were there, no one came out indicating that he was the leader of the Croatian forces. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: It's a small area. I suppose that had there been anything like that I would have seen it, and I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Can I deal, please, with the lights being shone into the hangar. I presume the lights were being shone into the hangar because it was dark; is that right? Dark outside.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was early dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, it was early dusk when you received the call. Isn't that right? But when you got there, was it not dark?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. One could say so. It was 10 to 15 minutes. That's what it took us to arrive there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they were all wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I can't be positive about all of them, but I didn't see a single person wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But you saw JNA uniforms around and in the hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be right to say you didn't see anyone making lists of the people at that time? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I wasn't really paying attention to the left side of the hangar. I didn't notice anyone noting anything down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you described "paralysed by fear", what do you mean by that? You used the phrase "paralysed by fear" in relation to one of them. Tell us his symptoms.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I called him out of the group, motivated by sincere motives. I could tell that he was an odd man in there. And when he came out, I felt really sorry for the man. Based on his face and body language, I could see that he was paralysed, that he was gripped by fear. So what I attempted to do was to restore his inner balance and to talk to him. So I put these frank questions to him about the problems, and I waited until he said what his problem was, and I said, "Is that the only problem?" And he said, "Yes." And he probably was wondering why I singled him out. He was afraid. He was afraid that something bad would happen to him and that I would something bad to him. I guess that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is said that you can smell fear. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it's an actual smell, but one can sense this -- this cramp that overcomes a person, the spasm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you agree that when you went into that hangar that that was the feel that you had from the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: One could see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, I saw that these were our people in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about our people. I'm talking that they were -- had that feel of fear. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were aware of their situation. They had surrendered. They were now wondering what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: They were uncertain about the future, awaiting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it is right to say that you were based originally in Negoslavci, and I think it is also correct to say that there were nine jeeps kept at Negoslavci. Is that right or not? In approximate numbers.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Eight jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Forgive me. What I would like to deal with is as follows: You were a driver. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the function of your driving was often to drive senior officers or staff officers around; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: You mean during the Vukovar events, during wartime, or what period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you for pointing out the imprecision of my question. Let's deal with what I will call peacetime and then wartime. Shall we do that? In peacetime when you were in Belgrade with the guards, is it right that you would occasionally, perhaps more than occasionally, drive officers around in your vehicle? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: This unit had an escort role. It escorted heads of states, foreign heads of states. It also was part of security detail of ministers of defence from other countries visiting Yugoslavia and travelling throughout its territory, and also it was part of security detail of military dignitaries visiting Yugoslavia. Other than that, we seldom drove officers, individual officers. There were such cases, but they were not frequent during peacetime. We would escort the Federal Secretary of Defence, who was actually minister of defence, and perhaps sometimes Chief of Staff or some other high officials, but seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in a unit like a Guards Unit, one tends to get to know who the officers are in that unit for very obvious reasons?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: The nature of our work was quite covert, so visually, yes, we knew the faces. But as for other details, we didn't really inquire about other units, nor did other units stick their noses into our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
