utterances.text: I just want to focus on the Guards Unit. Might I suggest that you would know who the officers would be either in the Guards Unit or attached to them and know usually their names? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us move on, then, to wartime. And I will use that phrase. Would it be right to say that when you got to Negoslavci and what I will call the hinterland of Negoslavci, you saw those officers occasionally or irregularly? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would come across them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you knew who an officer called Vukasinovic was?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mr. Vukasinovic, Ljubisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tell us about Mr. Vukasinovic, please, what you knew about him when you were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I knew Vukasinovic even before Vukovar. I knew him as an officer member of the Guards Brigade, one of the security officers. That's what they used to be referred to. As for some greater details, personal details regarding him, I didn't know that. He was quite an open man, very sociable, well respected by many. That's what I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suppose that would include -- your commander would know Vukasinovic as well, I presume.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Logic would imply that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of a man called Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because he was linked. What did you know of Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was also one of the members of the security department as it was known, one of the security officers, and he was a commander in Negoslavci. When I went to see those four people, my idea was to take these four people to him so he would see living examples, live examples of what they looked like and were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why would you take prisoners of war to the security organ? Can you just explain to me? I don't -- I just need that clarified for me.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: There was no other place where I could take them. That was my command, my command headquarters. In my view, that was the only appropriate place to take them, to hand them over to relevant officers. That was quite a unique case. We had no such cases previously, at least to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say the security organ or officers in the security organ can order members of the military police. That's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I'm not much of a soldier, but I was well aware of the chain of command in that area. As far as I know, it follows the military hierarchy, and a security organ can only issue a professional technical order. For example, I was a commander of the smallest military police units, and then a security organ comes along. As far as I'm aware, he would give professional, technical type of advice or orders, but I would normally receive orders from my immediate superior. It wasn't a practice to skip over those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it certainly happened occasionally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I can maybe entrap myself now, but it could have been a suggestion or some kind of advice on technical issues when it comes to escorting or security. And if a commander wasn't there and a security organ was, then in a way they were in charge of security issues and they could give some suggestions in that sense, from that perspective, but not concerning other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, of course not. But when they did do that, you obeyed as a dutiful soldier.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just deal with one or two other small topics. Your commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me for one moment? I just want to check something in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with your commander, and you know who I'm talking about. This can be dealt with, I hope, fairly briefly. I think it's right to say that at one stage there was a refusal, I think it was at Negoslavci, where 20 or 30 what I will call non-commissioned officers and officers indicated their refusal or reluctance to fight. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: In Serbian terminology the refusal and reluctance are two different things. Reluctance is not that bad you might say. In refusal, punishment would have been severe and there were no refusals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the word "reluctance"?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we tell, then, with the situation at Negoslavci where I believe 20 -- or I would suggest 20 or 30 non-commissioned officers and officers indicated their reluctance to fight? Now, can you tell us about that, please? What happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: What happened. Well, what happened is a relatively small number of professional soldiers were deployed along the front line, whereas the total numerical strength was quite considerable. Attacks were launched several times, and these attacks were spearheaded by a group known as Sareni. It was a special unit. Our support from the rear was getting less and less, as well as less frequent. At one point in time, we demanded that this entire thing be reorganised. That's one aspect of the situation. Secondly, I don't remember the exact date, but we hadn't had a change of clothes in quite some time. Our headquarters didn't provide for that. There was a natural reaction. People wanted to wash, wanted to have a bath. The first demand, the first request, it wasn't just reluctance. To be brutally frank, we just wanted to wash. And when we came forward with that, they withdrew us from the combat. They brought in a different unit and drove us back to Negoslavci. So what really happened, it was a mental thing, I suppose. It's difficult to understand. We then just eventually ended up not washing. We just all lay down on the floor and meditated for a while. That's how exhausted and stressed we were. And then the command people said, "You wanted to wash. Now you wouldn't wash. What did you mean exactly?" So the relations at this point were -- strained is going a bit too far, but there was certainly a misunderstanding that was soon smoothed over and we went back to our original position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not criticising. There is no suggestion of cowardice here in any way. I'm just trying to establish there was a meeting at Negoslavci where officers and non-commissioned officers indicated a reluctance to fight. Now, can I make the following suggestion to you: Is it right that you had some senior officers who came to persuade you to go back?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: At Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But they didn't make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did not Sljivancanin come to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Despite my best efforts, to be honest, believe me right now I can't remember if it was Sljivancanin or not, I know about a number of others, but I don't know about him. I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about Mrksic, did he come?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Vasiljevic come?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, General Vasiljevic. And in actual fact ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, you were saying, "In actual fact." I didn't interrupt you. You were saying, "General Vasiljevic. And in actual fact." Did you want to add something else?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said General Vasiljevic, a high-ranking military officer, I think he was a general at the time that enjoyed a high level of authority with that unit, and Colonel Mile Mrksic as our commander were two authoritative figures, and they certainly had the power to move us. There had been requests to fill in some vacancies and have some of our wounded soldiers replaced. There was a group of volunteers, seven or eight soldiers, and we returned at our commander's initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move forward in time? I think it is January, February, 1992. Do you accept from me that your commander was promoted at the start of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: 1992 is the year of our floundering, our failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, things happened in terms of appointments and removals, in terms of personnel, from that our military perspective made no sense at all. Technically, yes, perhaps. Technically, perhaps, he was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was being a professional soldier important to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: To me personally, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you aware of a gentleman known as Arkan at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You had never heard of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: At the time, yes, I'd heard the name mentioned, but it wasn't a resounding name at the time. It's not that people were in awe of him, at least not among us, among my circle. I don't know about the general environment, but this certainly applied to me. You see, I was in no situation to follow the media or the TV, that we were isolated from media reports to some extent, so probably that was one of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it not right that Arkan at that time had a reputation for ruthlessness?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking we heard that Arkan's men about coming in from the left, from Borovo and Luzac, and that's where the story ended as far as we were concerned. Given what exactly was going on we didn't really think there was fierce fighting over there but it's difficult to say because these are two opposite ends of Vukovar. It's difficult for us to say. We never met, and I don't think I have ever seen a single one of these Arkan's men who were allegedly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did it ever or did it never come to your ears that he and his soldiers committed atrocities or there were questionable acts by them? You never heard that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to stick to our original time line. I can't say I didn't hear about that, but if we focus on Vukovar, if we focus on 1991, the answer is no. At the time, I heard no such thing. Later on, needless to say, this became known. Stories became known and started spreading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What stories became known and started spreading about Arkan and his troops? And can you please remember that you've sworn to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I've sworn to tell the truth. That's what I'm here for. That is my principal reason for being here. Many members of our unit, myself included, did not have much respect for units of that kind such as Arkan's men. We sometimes came across each other, as was inevitable. And I do not wish to delve on rumours or interpret rumours. There was a lot being said in the press shown on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well. I will leave it. With regard to the TO, would it be right to say that they fought bravely on many occasions? The paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I did little together with paramilitary formations. We had professional soldiers in our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, what I would suggest to you with regard to the paramilitaries is as follows: There were many of them who fought bravely, but they had a reputation where they lacked discipline. They needed control. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure if I'm allowed to raise an objection. This is the first we've said about this. But I think counsel should define what he means by paramilitary units and what the witness means when he says TO. I think there is slippery ground and there may be some miscommunication between counsel and the witness. I think the way counsel has chosen not to define paramilitary units the witness will simply not know what he means. Maybe it's one thing for the OTP and another for the witness. It's not really an objection, but I thought this point needed raising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you have heard the issue. When we talk about irregular troops, and we can expand it, they fought bravely, but they had a problem with discipline. That was the problem at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Sir, in our area of combat operations, paramilitary units had no access. Anything that was outside the organic composition of the Guards Brigade would not have been allowed there. We did clash with them verbally several times, that sort of thing, and we did have incursions into our own rank and file, people who came there to loot, but in a matter of days such people would be expelled from our area of responsibility, and none of these would last too long. In our area, what now seems courage maybe meant no more than cowardice years ago, if you see what I mean. I'm a low-ranking soldier. I know about ground level. That's what I can tell you, the nitty-gritty but not the global thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's the nitty-gritty that I want to find out about. So, can you tell us, please, about the looting that was occurring?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Looting of property. I assume you mean that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like a picture, please, of the sort of problems that you were having with -- whatever phrase you want to use, with TOs or paramilitaries, and you mentioned looting. And I, just in very short order, to tell us exactly what type of problems you were having at that time. Now, you've told us they came into your area of responsibility. They shouldn't have done that, should they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: What I said is if anyone came to the area with intentions of that kind would not meet with much success in our area. Combat as raging at the time. Severe fighting was going on all the time. So you try to focus with all your military skill on surviving it, making it, and saving as many lives as you could of your fellow soldiers. It would have been preposterous to spend your time thinking about looting, to be quite frank. Most of us only wanted to get out of that hell alive. So much for looting as far as I'm concerned. I can only speak about my part of the unit, and I can tell you that this was certainly the case with us. That's how we worked. But if by looting mean looting, there was looting, yes. I had no clothes, for example, and I specifically did some looting. I would go into one of these houses and we would see some lingerie arranged nicely on a clothesline. Everything else around it had been ruined but there was all this underwear there. I would take off my own which was dirty by this time and put on some clean underwear. And then I would do the same thing five days later. That sort of thing. That's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think you know I'm not talking about your underwear or taking some clothes from a line. I'm asking you about the irregular behaviour of TOs or paramilitaries. Now, I'm simply suggesting to you that they had a reputation at that time as being sometimes brave fighters but also they were not well disciplined. That is correct, isn't it? That was the general reputation that they had. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I hold you in high esteem, don't get me wrong, but you're making me be brutally honest for the sake of the trial. I continued my career as a soldier after Vukovar, and I've had occasion to meet all sorts of different levels in the army, and one thing I can say before this Trial Chamber and before the general public, it's not only me, I venture to say 99 per cent of my fellow soldiers in their own area of responsibility such things could never have happened. You're quite right to claim that some of them were that way inclined. I mean, inclined to maybe grab something on the side, but these people were certainly not among us. Where were they? A lot of the Guards Brigade officers, when we returned later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that we've gone off track. I will return to Vukovar. Did you see Vukasinovic in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Not in Vukovar. I saw him in Negoslavci. But as for Vukovar, in town during combat operations, no, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Karanfilov in what I call the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I saw Karanfilov the day he was leading out Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was that before or after your trip to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Chronologically -- I know he was excited. He was saying that he had this very special task, and that's where the story ended. Later on when we met in Belgrade, he told me, he reminded me of that encounter and then said, "What happened afterwards?" At the time, I didn't know anything about Dr. Vesna and the trouble involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I put it this way: If we think of a time line, which is often the best way, that you saw Karanfilov with Dr. Vesna Bosanac, it was after that that you went to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest one or two things to you? You say that you went to Ovcara. Have you got any record of your visit to Ovcara, any documentary record?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, those who keep diaries, who keep logbooks, are usually in the rear. That's where they're normally stationed. I wouldn't say that I was always in the first line of combat, but I was exposed to severe risks, yes. And under those circumstances, my only focus was to survive and to ensure that I wouldn't make any omissions that would put at risk my fellow soldiers. So to tell you the truth, some chronology is completely mixed up in my mind. I think that some things happened later than they actually happened, and when people remind me, I just realise how wrong the chronology is in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you then when it was that you were first spoken to by presumably Mr. Vasic or Mr. Domazet? When were you first asked to give evidence in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I saw this gentleman last night for the first time, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. We knew about that.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I saw him some five to six days ago. We saw each other twice. He took my passport so that he could get my visa, and then I saw him when he needed my photographs for the visa. It was all quite hasty. He just took the photographs. And to tell you the truth I was taken by surprise. He, or rather, Mr. Lakcevic asked me somewhat informally earlier, "Stevan, would you agree to go and testify about the Ovcara events?" And I said, "Yes, of course." I'm not testifying for anybody. I'm testifying in order to establish the truth about the events in which I participated. And the story at the time was I would provide a written statement about the events, about how I went to the commander and so on. Later on, it expanded and they said, "Maybe you'll testify via videolink." And in the last four to five days they asked me whether I was prepared to come here before this Honourable Chamber and to tell the story here, and I said there's no reason for me to ignore the truth, to evade it, and no problem, I'll go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You said that you were to provide a written statement. Did you make a written statement or notes from your own memory before you spoke to the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. No. It's not my custom to keep notes or to keep a diary. And I regretted. Perhaps I should have noted things down on the paper. There were many traumatic, difficult events there, and one tends to forget it. Therefore, I am telling you that I regret that I didn't note anything down. By some chance I went back to Vukovar in 1993. I told you that I went back there as a member of the Guards Brigade. It was a moral obligation that I had, because I was born there. So I went back. And what was my idea then? My idea was to ensure that evil wouldn't be repeated. And then I heard that -- and it was true. It was a true fact. I don't know if it was recorded anywhere. I think that the commander is aware of the details. I think that even -- that he even suggested it to me, that a young man died in the vicinity --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I want to just go back to the topic I was on. I'm sure Mr. Domazet will ask you about 1993. Would you mind if I kept on the same topic? You've told us that you were approached to give evidence. You didn't make a written statement, but is there a written statement signed by you that has been compiled? Really, your account of what happened.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Pardon, but during what time? During what time do you mean that I signed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Your Honours, now it is suggested to the witness -- rather, the witness said that he gave no statement and that there was no statement that he ever gave, and now it is put to him whether he ever signed a statement. I don't see on the basis of what the Prosecutor is suggesting that he signed some statement. No statement exists, and I think that the witness is now all confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't think there was any ground for confusion there. Mr. Moore, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to just work out in sequence is you hadn't compiled a statement before going to the lawyers or investigator. When you got there and you started giving your story, was it a case of you just telling it straight out or -- I think you told us earlier on, about five minutes ago, that sometimes you were quite naturally confused, and then, as it were, it became realigned. Can you just tell us how it was it arose or how it happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: You mean my encounter with the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I received a call from Mr. Lakcevic. He asked to meet with me to talk about something, and I said what, and he said the events in Vukovar and around Vukovar in 1991. And I said gladly. I didn't know who Mr. Lakcevic was, whether he was Mr. Mrksic's lawyer or perhaps a counsel for the Prosecution. I didn't know anything about it. So we met, and he asked me about the unit in which I served. I gave him my personal details, and I told him that I was there, that I was in Vukovar, that there was nothing to conceal, that I was a soldier. He didn't ask me much. He asked me in which unit I served, what I knew about Ovcara, and I told him the story, the story about that event, that I knew about fact. Then we parted, and he didn't really say anything concrete to me as to what I would have to do later on. He said, "Would you confirm this if necessary?" And I said, "Yes. Why not?" And that's where the story ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Later on, he said, "If needed --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt you. If needed he would contact you, I presume. Is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what I would like to know, what parts of your account or your story were you confused about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I didn't know technically the process, how the testimony would transpire, whether I would be providing a written statement and that would be the end of my evidence, or whether -- because that was the initial idea. They said, "If in the view of the team," and I wasn't sure who was the relevant team, I would testify via videolink. And then it turned out that I would be a live witness. And I came here totally unprepared. I met the gentleman yesterday and that's the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just repeat to you what you've said to this Court. It's what you said earlier on. "So to tell you the truth, some chronology is completely mixed up in my mind. I think that some things happened later than they actually happened, and when people remind me, I just realise how wrong the chronology is in my mind." I want to know about what people were reminding you about to assist your memory.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, sir, Mr. Prosecutor, not relating to this topic. These are just marginal issues, issues that occasionally come up. In Serbia, we do not have any services dealing with post-traumatic stress disorders. The way we resolve this is we get together and we help each other deal with the stress through talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I'm going to repeat what you said. "So to tell you the truth, some chronology is completely mixed up in my mind. When people remind me, I just realise how wrong the chronology is in my mind." I am simply asking you which -- which parts are mixed up. Why should you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, you put questions to me and this is how we came to that particular topic. I was referring to some things which after the passage of time became significant. I know of an event, but, for example, I forgot the date or I forgot the name of a person, which is quite a natural consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, absolutely fair -- you see, your commander gave evidence and thought that the Ovcara matter occurred on the 20th, not the 18th. Would you accept that as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. No. Not at all. It was definitely on the 18th, for a number of reasons, and here's why -- I don't know what else you want me to say to corroborate this. This pig or piglet, it wasn't really that we were celebrating a major victory, no. It was a spontaneous reaction of a group of people rejoicing that they survived. They wanted to mark the end of this agony which lasted for as long as it lasted. This was, for example, one of the details. We went there as the meat was being roasted. After we finished with Ovcara, we returned and then we ate that and spent time together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you have nothing at all that you can rely on for the date, apart from your memory 15 years later on. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: This is a watershed in what was going on, this and the 2nd of October and a number of other dates that remain etched deep in my memory. The 2nd of October is the date of incursion. On the 12th we had a great number of casualties. On the 16th, just as well. Some of my fellow soldiers were killed. So these are some of the dates that remain with me, including the 18th for that very reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I then ask you this question: You say that you know Major Vukasinovic and you have accepted logically and sensibly so did your manager. When you went to Ovcara, whatever date it was, forget whether it's the 18th, forget whether it's the 20th, how long do you think you remained at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't be very specific about that. It was an hour altogether or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see Major Vukasinovic when you were there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't. I know him. He has very striking features, and I didn't see him. As for officers, I saw our commander who I had arrived there with. I saw this young lad the police officer who was waiting for me there. There may have been others. I wasn't looking at their ranks. But it was our unit and the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you -- you never saw Vukasinovic, and you never saw your commander speak to Vukasinovic. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: My commander, my commander, remained in the first half, just as we entered, you know. We took that door, and he was in that first area. I didn't see him further down. He was around there or at the door. I was the last to leave the hangar. I was the last, literally the last, because I was dealing with -- I was dealing with talking to that man at the far end. I spent about 15 or 20 minutes talking to that man, the man whom I'd taken outside. Did anyone else come in the meantime while I was away is not something I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with it this way: I assume you didn't Karanfilov there either. You didn't see Vukasinovic and you didn't see Karanfilov; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you say this as an honest witness?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've said, "I didn't." Does that mean that you've heard that other people did?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Thank you for paying me that compliment. I am an honourable witness, indeed, but I didn't see him, and I heard nobody say that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You never heard your commander say that he had to speak to Vukasinovic, this friend of yours, and was told to leave? Is that what you're saying as an honest witness?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I don't know what decided the commander for us to be off. I suppose it was the fact, as we had all seen, that the TO were there, the people who had surrendered, and they were being secured by the military police. We saw nothing irregular or unusual happening, and things were going the way they were going, and there was no need for our presence there, so we just turned around, got back into our vehicles. And I spent the entire evening with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to me why it was if nothing was happening that you spent, as you believe, about an hour there? Because there was no need for you to remain, was there? And you had a pig on the roast. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a party that we were leaving. I'll tell you what took us so long. The power generator that had to be connected that took quite some time. We didn't just get there and turn round -- only to turn round and leave immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I myself spent 20 minutes talking to that Croat that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question I'm asking and others may ask is if there was nothing going on, why is it a specialist unit remains, as you believe, for an hour? The power generator's got nothing to do with you because the military police are there. So what's a specialist unit staying there for that length of time? No need for it, is there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again. I wasn't being very specific when I said an hour. Give or take ten minutes. I think that is an acceptable aberration given how much time has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we're at the break time. I have literally 15 minutes cross-examination left, but I do want to take my time on it, but we will finish easily today. Would this be an appropriate moment for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is well and truly appropriate. I thought you were near finished so I ran on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have redactions. We will resume at a quarter past the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, we haven't much longer to go you'll be pleased to hear. One or two additional topics. I want to ask you about Major Sljivancanin, who was head of the security organ in the Vukovar area. You were aware of that fact at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We probably can deal with this fairly quickly. Would it be right to say that the English phrase that he was a security officer who moved around a lot in and around the front line and general areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: It's a matter of how you phrase it, yes, but I did see him a couple of times. For an officer of that level, yes, you might put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, "For an officer of that level, yes, you might put it that way"? Explain to us, please. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: It is not usual to have officers along the front line among the soldiers who are high-ranking officers. It's a rare occurrence. I think it applies to every conflict. Major Sljivancanin is indisputably a brave officer. He was fearless when it came to touring the front line soldiers. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that he was moving in a way that you don't expect the security organ to -- to visit these areas? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I think that goes back some way. Just before everything started in Vukovar, Major Sljivancanin had been appointed a security officer, but he changed a lot of jobs in the Anti-Terrorist Unit, so maybe there was an emotional side to the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that Major Sljivancanin, you've said about him being brave, that he was a good officer, he knew what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: He had some virtues that distinguished him as any other officer, and I knew him from before we went to Vukovar. We took our first military steps together, as it were. He was an officer. I remained an NCO. We met at various levels. At a lower level once he was even my commander. I know that he was an equitable and well-respected officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. I asked why did you come to the conclusion that he knew what was happening on the ground in Vukovar? Was it because he was an efficient officer who moved around? Is that why you give the answer?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I can hardly be able to -- I can hardly be expected to say. I myself and a lot of others were surprised to see him move around quite freely in an area where there were daily casualties and quite many too. That was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And would it be right to say that it's not from your own personal knowledge but from the reputation that you heard from other soldiers on the ground? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, we were not a panel evaluating other officers. It wasn't down to us to assess what their respective abilities were, but that was the impression that prevailed. I suppose you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's also right, I think, he even has a nickname in relation to his participation in Vukovar. Isn't that right? Isn't he known as either the Black Dog or the Black Knight of Vukovar? I can't remember which one, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're making me laugh. It's a sad story, but you've just managed to make me laugh. The Black Dog, did you say? The Black Dog.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I'm suggesting is he was well known for his partition in Vukovar. He was either called the Black Dog of Vukovar or the Black Knight. Perhaps it's the Black Knight as opposed to the Dog. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Who? Who called him that, the Black Knight of Vukovar, the enemy? We ourselves? No, not there. Not in Vukovar. I really didn't. While everything was going on in Vukovar, I didn't. I truly didn't. Later, perhaps, the press, they were trying to blow things out of proportion. You know what they do. I'm not sure how it went, but it certainly wasn't something I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with what you heard at the time. Would it be right that you heard about the killings at Ovcara, or perhaps a better way of putting it, when's the first time you heard about the killings at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: If there was any blemish on my conscience, I would certainly be looking for a way to conceal that. I would not be able to summon up the courage that it takes to face this Tribunal. So the Chamber must believe me. The crime that was committed at Ovcara was something that I first read about in the press when this started being brought up in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was that, a year later, six months?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Much later. Many years later. I returned to Vukovar in 1993, and no one I knew in Vukovar gave me even an inkling of anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You never heard from anyone about rumours of atrocities? Because can I just suggest to you that I think it's right to say that other people heard rumours about atrocities the following day. But you heard nothing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I said that we members of that unit enjoyed utmost respect by almost everyone. These people didn't start discussions with us about what was going on on the other side of the law, if I may put it that way. There were no hints even, knowing that every single one of our members was extremely professional and would have taken steps. I assure you that I heard nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you ever given a statement or spoken to anyone involving an investigation of the Ovcara killings before the Defence actually spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never discussed it with anyone, and I'm really not informed when it comes to these events. I know the persons who were convicted by the court in Belgrade. Out of those persons I know several, but there was not a single hint. There was nothing in anyone's conduct that would indicate to me that something on that scale took place. In fact, for a long time I didn't believe in this until there was a critical mass of information in the papers, because, you know, stories can be amplified, blown out of proportion, or to the contrary. The significance can be reduced. You know how these things happen. And I knew only what the press wrote about, and then when the trial started I was very surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you involved in the clean-up of bodies around Vukovar at any time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a soldier, I suggest served with you, called Aziz Memic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it right to say that Aziz Memic went with you to Ovcara on that evening?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I mentioned Memic as the person whom Big Dzo approached when he told him --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so it was Memic who was approached. Do you know where Memic is at this time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. No. Truly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: A guards regiment, perhaps in certain places, often has an association for former soldiers or officers. Did the -- or does the Guards Brigade or regiment have a former -- or a club for its former soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: We had dramatic political changes which affected the situation, so the system of associations and clubs fell apart. In the old Yugoslavia, we had an old tradition of assembling former members of units and so on. In my unit, the tradition was to assemble on the day Tito died. We would get together and then go our separate ways. And there was an idea to do the same in this new unit, but officially it was never implemented, because they didn't want us to cause any trouble or to -- to affect the new trend. So as a result, there were no attempts to reinstate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that you have not met any former Guards soldier, non-commissioned officer or officer recently?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't put it that way. Occasionally, yes, but as for Memic specifically, I can't even recall the last time I saw him. I can't even remember seeing him after 1991. I heard from my friends that he left the service and was quite poor, because as an honourable officer, he didn't dare go back to Bosnia. He's a Muslim, and he would be exposed to certain dangers there. In Serbia, how he lives nowadays in Serbia, I really don't know, but I heard that his life wasn't easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you find out or did you hear where it was he was living? The area.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, really not. I heard that he used to repair blinds or some wooden objects, but this is really not reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just about finished, but I just want to deal with one personal matter, and I'm sorry I have to put it but I will. It's right, is it not, that you are a man who especially around 1991 and afterwards had a fairly significant drinking problem? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Which year? I apologise. Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, before we go to which year, which year do you say you had a drinking problem?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I would kindly ask you to rephrase your question. Could you repeat your initial question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will for you. I would suggest that you're a man who, unfortunately, has had occasion to drink large amounts of alcohol, that you're a heavy drinker. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Everybody has occasions. Alcohol is available to all adults. Everybody has occasions to drink, drink a lot. If somebody wants to do it excessively, then, yes, they have occasions to do that. What you're doing to me I consider to be dishonourable, but in view of this Trial Chamber, I will tell the truth. In 1993, when I returned back to Vukovar there was nothing going on there, almost nothing. It was mostly restaurants and bars that were open, nothing else, and due to poor food we were receiving, I did tend to drop by a bar often, but I'm not sure that I would phrase it in those terms as you did, because had I drunk all those quantities, I would have been paralysed nowadays. I'm 52 years old, and I stopped drinking in 1997. I haven't had a drop to drink since then. And had I met you at the time, I would have had a drink with you, as I did with all descent people. Mr. Van Lynden, after we parted, gave me as a present a bottle of whisky with inscriptions "SkyNews" on the bottle. Maybe it was him who put me on that path.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So would it be right to say, then, that Mr. Van Lynden gave you alcohol because you were a man who was drinking quite a lot when you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. These are serious matters. I told you that when we parted, he did that. He wasn't trying to turn that encounter into something ironic. Mr. Lynden gave such a present to my commander, Muslim; to a Croat; and to me, a Serb. Each of us got one, as well as a videotape of SkyNews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I suggest to you what actually happened? I'm suggesting to you that you're almost correct in many of the things that you have said, that in actual fact it was not the 18th that you went to Ovcara, it was the 20th, that you went with your commander, you went with Memic as well, and it was there that Vukasinovic and Karanfilov were in control of those prisoners. Now, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: This is your view. You're entitled to one. I have full respect for it, but these are the facts that I eyewitnessed, experienced personally, and I support them with my whole being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I would suggest that in actual fact that there were groups of TO at that time who were both in and around that hangar. Now, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I could see, although it was dark, but they were not among the people that I saw, nowhere in our vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I will have to go beyond our usual sitting hours, quarter to 2.00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we can fortunately sit on for a little while now with the cooperation of the staff. I wouldn't worry about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. It won't take long. I think we'll go beyond just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Bisic, just a few questions about what Mr. Moore examined you. First of all, I think it was suggested to you that the order that you received from the commander when you were told to go to Ovcara, that it was a result of a rumour. First of all, tell me, was it an order which pertained to you as a group or was it really a rumour that was spread around?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No. There was nobody else. That group was there by itself. And that particular period of time was a bit more relaxed. We weren't in a spasm as earlier. And as they started roasting that piglet, we began talking, joking, consoling each other, if I may call it that. At one point, (redacted) said, "Let's go." We asked him, "Where, commander? Go where?" He said -- I can't quote his words verbatim now, but the essence of that was, "Let's go. It seems that something is happening there."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to Mr. Moore's questions, you mentioned an event involving Karanfilov and Dr. Bosanac. It wasn't quite clear to me whether you saw that with your own eyes or whether you heard about it later from Karanfilov. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: I knew Karanfilov as a junior officer from the Guards. Somehow it happened that I didn't see him much during Vukovar events. At one point I saw him. I greeted him, and I was surprised by the cold reception. He just passed by me, and that surprised me. I was wondering how come my fellow soldier, a friend, couldn't spare even a minute to greet me. And I reminded him of that later, and he said that he was on a very important mission at that point in time, and it was much later that I -- that I heard that he had to do something with Mrs. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So you heard that from him. You didn't see it yourself.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Another question pertaining to your relations with Witness P001. You confirmed, and we heard that before, that you helped this man a great deal and that you went together with Bosnia under dangerous circumstances to get some relatives of his. My question is this: You were obviously on very good terms with him at the time. After his departure, did he ever get in touch with you and, if no, why not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: My answer was in the affirmative to that question, and these were the events that really shook me. This was a man who is very dear to me, and I would say something briefly about his motives. His wife felt deserted. She had a twin sister in that area, in Jajce, and they were experiencing a lot of trouble. So the wife pressured my commander, saying that he had done a lot for the country, for the people, but nothing for her. He and I would spend a lot of nights in informal chats, and on one occasion - I wasn't drunk. I really wasn't drunk - I promised his sister that I would bring back her -- I promise his wife that I would bring back her sister and her family. And he didn't want to let me go by myself. He was quite rational about it. He was saying that I was going to a high-danger area and so on. So we went there, and I brought the sister of his wife, her husband and children, plus another child who was orphaned, a Serb child who was orphaned. At that time it was tremendously risky to move in the way that we travelled there. We travelled in a private vehicle. They were in civilian clothes, and my commander and I were in military clothes, and we had to go through many checkpoints, and there was a great danger that Muslims would stop us. So it was quite miraculous that we passed threw. When we passed through the danger zone they asked me -- the husband of the sister asked me, "Are we now on free territory?" I said, "Yes." And then all five of them started singing. They started singing a song called "One Day in Life." And later I helped them get passports. I had some connections, and back in 1991 it was still possible. Then they left. I don't know where they went, but they left the country. My address never changed. All my details are in the phone book. They're public. They never got in touch with me, never called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just tell me one thing. When you say -- which country were they in that they were free?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: We crossed a bridge to go into Serbia, and once we crossed that bridge, the border, he assumed that we were in Serbia -- or, rather, in Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple of questions left. In reply to one of Mr. Moore's questions, you told him what you knew about what had occur at Ovcara during the night between the 20th and 21st. You said you first found out in the media. Is that your answer? You did not have any personal information concerning that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one last thing. The date has been questioned, not the fact that you were there. You explained the chronology of that day. Do you still stand by your previous statement that it only could have been the 18th, that is the day of Vukovar's fall?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN BISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. You'll be pleased to know, Mr. Bisic, that that completes the questions for you, so that there will be no further need for you to attend here, and when convenient arrangements are made, it will be possible for you to return to your place of living. We would like to thank you very much for your attendance here and the assistance that you've given to us. We would also like to thank all those who have stayed on a little late to enable us to finish the evidence of this witness. We will now adjourn, and we resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
